  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- What is painted stays painted. There is no undo: paint over what you
  don't want.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count. The
  clock isn't a budget or a target.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by reflecting,
  flipping, rotating or translating another mask's or stroke's coordinates.
  A shape that mirrors another is drawn as its own shape, not as
  `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or `m:at(W - x, y)`.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/friedrich_materials.md (his materials and method, sourced);
notes/research/trees.md (how trees are built) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
- You make every artistic decision.
- Look at your painting often, whole and close up.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  Entries stay as written.
- Develop the painting until you judge it complete.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

Each film dries at its own pace, set by its pigments, its thickness and
its oil. Thin lean paint of fast-drying pigments is touch-dry in a day;
thick, oily paint of slow pigments can stay open for weeks. Wet paint
under a new stroke comes up into it; paint laid over dry paint sits on
top of it.

** Each chunk is its own Lua chunk:
  `p = pile{...}` is there in later chunks, `local p = ...` is not.
- **Randomness is deterministic.** `math.random`, `rand` and `randn` are
  reseeded at the start of every chunk from the canvas's seed and the
  chunk's number, and passes pick their own seeds the same way (pass
  `seed=` to fix one). A replay paints the same thing, and a failed chunk
  doesn't shift the next one's randomness.
- **No OS access.** `io`, `os`, `debug`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile`
  and `collectgarbage` aren't there. `print` goes to the reply.
- **Lua 5.5.** Numbers are integers or floats (`7 // 2` is 3, `7 / 2` is
  3.5). Bitwise operators are built in; there is no `unpack` (use
  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode).
- **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
  Tables keyed by strings, numbers and booleans walk in Lua's order; a
  table with any other key walks in a fixed order (booleans, numbers,
  strings, then other keys in the order they were made). For a big list,
  `ipairs` is faster.
- **Memory.** A mask costs 4 bytes a pixel, a form 28. Keep big things
  `local` when later chunks don't need them.

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. Entries already there stay as they were written; writing a note
doesn't advance painting time.

38. The blender fuses open paint by lifting it and moving it. It can't move

39. `blend` stays inside its mask by default. Unclipped, it drags wet paint

    blending pass stay on top as a lacy texture.

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting (stiff, barely blends) to
    tacky to touch-dry. Lead-white-rich paint gels in about 2 hours and
    average paint in about 3.5. A lean coat is touch-dry in about a day;
    bone black and lakes take days. Thick or oily paint dries slower.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers
    it.

-- Cluster centers along the living branches of the Ancient Oak
local oak_leaf_clusters = {
  -- Eastern Bough
  {380, 298, 12}, {400, 272, 14}, {418, 246, 12}, {430, 222, 10},
  {444, 294, 12}, {466, 272, 14}, {485, 246, 12}, {500, 226, 10},

  {162, 316, 12}, {142, 336, 14}, {122, 350, 12}, {108, 366, 10},
  {100, 252, 12}, {86, 236, 10}, {72, 218, 8},
  {248, 320, 10}, {228, 296, 10}, {210, 275, 10}
}

  {754, 255, 10}, {760, 222, 10}, {720, 198, 10}, {734, 154, 8}
}

local function paint_cluster(cx, cy, radius, n)
  for i = 1, n do
    local ang = rand(0, 6.28)
    local r = rand(0, radius)
    local x = cx + r * math.cos(ang)
    local y = cy + r * math.sin(ang)
    local drag_len = rand(1.2, 2.8)
    local drag_ang = rand(0.8, 1.8) -- hanging downward
    
    -- Pick color randomly with natural weighting
    local p
    local roll = rand(0, 1)
    if roll < 0.4 then
      p = p_leaf_dark
    elseif roll < 0.75 then
      p = p_leaf_russet
    else
      p = p_leaf_gold
    end
    
    b_leaf:load(p, 0.7)
    b_leaf:touch(x, y, {pressure=rand(0.4, 0.75), drag={drag_len, drag_ang}, twist=rand(-0.3, 0.3)})
  end
end

-- Paint Ancient Oak clusters
for _, cl in ipairs(oak_leaf_clusters) do

end

-- Paint Companion Tree clusters
for _, cl in ipairs(comp_leaf_clusters) do

end

**Analyzing the Evidence**

Okay, I've got it. The image `look-0039.png` is key. My focus is now zeroed in on the trunk. It's clear the fill was executed via `work(m_trunk, {hand="body", ...})`, which employed a mosaic of round filbert brush dabs. This is crucial for understanding the overall technique. Now, the branch...


**Defining the Techniques**

I'm now zeroing in on the specific techniques revealed by close examination. The collar details – those dark circles at branch junctions – are clear, and the oval hollow, the spoke-like roots, and the wire-like shoots are all essential. The limbs, as straight grey tubes with circular collars at their bases, further complete this detailed breakdown. The `look` command proved essential to break down the composition to its essential elements.


**Refining the Details**

I'm now revising my understanding of the branch collars and hollow cavity based on Alex Shigo's insights. The collars aren't simple circles, but a seamless flow of trunk wood around the branch base. The cavity is also not a clean oval, but a rough, decaying opening. Also, I need to rethink the roots as muscular buttresses, not spoke lines. My focus has also shifted to the Dolmen. I need to get rid of the yellow circle, and I am planning to replace it with cool granite grains, subtle moss, and ancient chips. I need to make the chamber darker.

events.text: Close inspection (look-0038 and look-0039) provides indispensable guidance. The trunk previously showed filbert body dabs, target-like collar circles, and an overly geometric hollow. In nature and Friedrich's art, oak bark consists of powerful longitudinal, interlocking vertical furrows and ridges that flow organically from swelling root buttresses up into the limbs. The hollow is an irregular, weathered fissure framed by rounded wound-wood calluses, and the dolmen's chamber must be a deep, solemn cavern of absolute darkness. We now sculpt the trunk with continuous longitudinal strokes of raw umber, bone black, and ochre, sculpt the callused hollow, and render the dolmen as monumental ancient granite.

I've been further refining the paint mixtures. Specifically, I adjusted the ratios for `p_bark_dark`, `p_bark_light`, `p_hollow_void`, and `p_woundwood`, and updated medium amounts. The goal is to get the color, texture, and light interaction just right. Then, I'll focus on the actual application with the correct brush strokes. My next steps are to apply vertical strokes, and shape the hollow.


**Detailing Root Buttresses**

I'm now focusing on the oak's root buttresses. I'm aiming for broad, swelling ridges that flare outwards and disappear into the ground. I'm also planning the hollow details, which features jagged, rotting wood (`p_hollow_void`) with a rounded callus lip (`p_woundwood` and `p_bark_light`) on each side.
I'm also working on the Dolmen. I will deepen the chamber void between the uprights using `p_hollow_void`. I'll resurface the capstone with weathered granite color (`p_stone_mid`), sculpting the top to catch the twilight and casting deep shadows. Finally, I will restate the upright orthostats.

events.text:
***Hünengrab im Abendlicht*** *(Megalithic Tomb in Evening Light)*

Painted in oil on fine linen over a traditional two-layer ground—a warm ochre-red earth knife ground leveled across the weave beneath a thin, brushed lead-white preparation—this landscape embodies the quiet, solemn spirit of German Romanticism in the manner of Caspar David Friedrich. 

Upon a desolate, windswept coastal barrow in late autumn, an ancient megalithic stone tomb (*Hünengrab*) rests in eternal stillness. Its weathered Scandinavian granite capstone and supporting orthostats frame a deep, mysterious burial chamber, sheltered beneath the powerful arching bough of a veteran, hollowed oak (*Quercus robur*). The ancient tree exhibits the natural poetry of old-age retrenchment: while its lower muscular limbs reach in protective reverence over the prehistoric grave, its upper crown has died back into stark, bleached stag-horn antlers that spear into the quiet, cold cobalt-smalt firmament. Beyond the dark ridge crest, where dried carline thistle skeletons stand against a glowing band of valley mist, the vast evening sky rises seamlessly from a radiant primrose and amber afterglow at the horizon into the sublime stillness of the twilight zenith. In the foreground, an ancient sandy pilgrim path winds through the undulating heather and scattered glacial erratic boulders, inviting the solitary wanderer to meditate upon time, mortality, and the enduring silence of nature.

    edge.
46. `ribbon` puts a round disc at every point, both ends included, so it
    reaches half a width past its end points.
47. Two separately softened masks that meet leave a light gap or a dark
    overlap along the seam. A mask and its inverse (`m` and `-m`) meet
    without one.
48. A passage bounded by a mask shows a cut edge wherever its paint differs
    from its neighbor's at the mask's edge.

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting (stiff, barely blends) to
    tacky to touch-dry. Lead-white-rich paint gels in about 2 hours and
    average paint in about 3.5. A lean coat is touch-dry in about a day;
    bone black and lakes take days. Thick or oily paint dries slower.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers
    it.

Now that the canvas is dry, I'm shifting my focus to the artistic vision. I'm reviewing the brief, Friedrich's research, and the requirements. My goal is to synthesize these elements to understand the desired outcome.

I need to synthesize his techniques with my own.


**Reimagining Friedrich's Palette**

I'm now completely dissatisfied with the current canvas. The colors and shapes are all wrong, especially the sky. I envision a vast, luminous sky with a glowing afterglow at the horizon, transitioning from amber to silver and deep twilight. The trees need organic, flowing forms, not rigid diagrams.

I'm now focusing on the atmospheric depth. I envision serene cobalt and smalt blue at the zenith, transitioning to a luminous twilight. I'm now zeroing in on the composition's key element: the megalithic tomb.   {x=900, y=458}, {x=1020, y=474}
}

local function barrow_crest(x)
  if x <= crest_nodes[1].x then return crest_nodes[1].y end
  if x >= crest_nodes[#crest_nodes].x then return crest_nodes[#crest_nodes].y end
  for i = 1, #crest_nodes - 1 do
    local p0 = crest_nodes[i]
    local p1 = crest_nodes[i+1]
    if x >= p0.x and x <= p1.x then

local function barrow_crest(x)
  if x <= barrow_nodes[1].x then return barrow_nodes[1].y end
  if x >= barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].x then return barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].y end
  for i = 1, #barrow_nodes - 1 do
    local p0 = barrow_nodes[i]
    local p1 = barrow_nodes[i+1]
    if x >= p0.x and x <= p1.x then

      local s = u * u * (3 - 2 * u)
      return p0.y + s * (p1.y - p0.y)

  end
  return 450

local barrow_nodes = {
  {x=-20, y=468}, {x=80, y=462}, {x=180, y=452}, {x=270, y=435},
  {x=340, y=422}, {x=385, y=416}, {x=450, y=422}, {x=520, y=436},
  {x=600, y=452}, {x=680, y=454}, {x=760, y=440}, {x=830, y=440},
  {x=910, y=452}, {x=1020, y=468}
}

local function barrow_crest(x)
  if x <= barrow_nodes[1].x then return barrow_nodes[1].y end
  if x >= barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].x then return barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].y end
  for i = 1, #barrow_nodes - 1 do
    local p0 = barrow_nodes[i]
    local p1 = barrow_nodes[i+1]
    if x >= p0.x and x <= p1.x then
      local u = (x - p0.x) / (p1.x - p0.x)
      local s = u * u * (3 - 2 * u)
      return p0.y + s * (p1.y - p0.y)
    end
  end
  return 445
end

-- 1. Mathematical spline for the noble prehistoric barrow crest
local barrow_nodes = {
  {x=-20, y=465}, {x=80, y=458}, {x=180, y=448}, {x=260, y=430},
  {x=330, y=415}, {x=385, y=408}, {x=445, y=414}, {x=520, y=430},
  {x=600, y=448}, {x=680, y=450}, {x=760, y=436}, {x=830, y=436},
  {x=910, y=448}, {x=1020, y=465}
}

local function barrow_crest(x)
  if x <= barrow_nodes[1].x then return barrow_nodes[1].y end
  if x >= barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].x then return barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].y end
  for i = 1, #barrow_nodes - 1 do
    local p0 = barrow_nodes[i]
    local p1 = barrow_nodes[i+1]
    if x >= p0.x and x <= p1.x then
      local u = (x - p0.x) / (p1.x - p0.x)
      local s = u * u * (3 - 2 * u)
      return p0.y + s * (p1.y - p0.y)
    end
  end
  return 440
end

  if x >= barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].x then return barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].y end
  for i = 1, #barrow_nodes - 1 do

    local p1 = barrow_nodes[i+1]
    if x >= p0.x and x <= p1.x then

      local s = u * u * (3 - 2 * u)
      return p0.y + s * (p1.y - p0.y)
    end
  end
  return 440

It transforms into a scene called *Hünengrab im Abendlicht*, showcasing a megalithic tomb atop a barrow. The emphasis now shifts to the monument, the evening light, and the Baltic landscape.


**Embracing Romanticism's Essence**

I'm now fully immersed in the spirit of German Romanticism. The goal is to capture its purity and emotional power, free from any distracting or amateurish elements. I'm carefully rereading BRIEF.md to ensure I'm adhering to its guidelines, especially the instruction to avoid reference images and the constraint to work directly without an undo function. The emphasis now is on creating a truly timeless landscape.


**Reimagining the Scene**

I'm now completely unshackled. BRIEF.md doesn't mandate trees at all; it's all invention! The "slingshot tree" was an awkward distraction. I've covered it, transforming the image. Now, the sky dominates, vast and serene, drawing the eye to a monumental megalithic tomb and a Baltic barrow. The waxing crescent moon and evening star create an awe-inspiring, solemn atmosphere.


**Envisioning the Foreground**

I'm now focusing on the foreground elements. I'm replacing the highway with glacial erratics, heather, and peaty hollows, which is so much more authentic and beautiful! The goal is to capture simplicity, solemnity, vastness, and eternity, in the style of Friedrich. I'm working to cover those clumsy tree shapes with the sky, and then the heather and barrow.


**Structuring the Composition**

I'm now contemplating a two-chunk approach. Chunk 99 will be devoted to establishing the twilight sky, Baltic coast, evening mist, and celestial bodies. Then I'll focus on laying down the barrow mound and rolling peaty heathland across the foreground. I recall how efficiently I sculpted the dolmen earlier, and plan to execute the dolmen in Chunk 100. My goal is to work fast and clean for a crisp, granite-textured megalith.

-- 2. Sky Piles

blend(rect(0, 432, 1000, 34), {angle=0})

-- 7. Waxing crescent moon and solitary evening star (Venus)
local p_moon_pure = pile{{"lead white", 34}, {"yellow ochre", 1.0}, {"chrome yellow", 0.4}, medium=0.12}
local b_rigger = brush{kind="round", width=1.3, point=1, stiffness=0.85}

b_rigger:stroke({
  {645.2, 105.5}, {641.5, 108.0}, {639.0, 112.5}, {640.2, 117.0}, {644.0, 119.5}
}, {pressure={0.08, 0.85, 1.0, 0.8, 0.08}, ramps={0.05, 0.05}})

local b_star = brush{kind="round", width=1.0, point=1, stiffness=0.9}
b_star:load(p_moon_pure, 1.0)
b_star:touch(688, 148, {pressure=0.6})

-- 8. The Noble Prehistoric Barrow Mound
local barrow_nodes = {
  {x=-20, y=465}, {x=80, y=458}, {x=180, y=448}, {x=260, y=430},
  {x=330, y=415}, {x=385, y=408}, {x=445, y=414}, {x=520, y=430},
  {x=600, y=448}, {x=680, y=450}, {x=760, y=436}, {x=830, y=436},
  {x=910, y=448}, {x=1020, y=465}
}

local function barrow_crest(x)
  if x <= barrow_nodes[1].x then return barrow_nodes[1].y end
  if x >= barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].x then return barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].y end
  for i = 1, #barrow_nodes - 1 do
    local p0 = barrow_nodes[i]
    local p1 = barrow_nodes[i+1]
    if x >= p0.x and x <= p1.x then
      local u = (x - p0.x) / (p1.x - p0.x)
      local s = u * u * (3 - 2 * u)
      return p0.y + s * (p1.y - p0.y)
    end
  end
  return 440

end
b_crest:stroke(crest_line, {pressure=0.9, ramps={0.01, 0.01}})

**Analyzing the Structure Change**

I've been examining the image closely. The udders are definitely absent now, replaced by two stone pillars. The space between the pillars forms a dark, empty chamber, and the overall impression is that of a concrete WWII bunker. There is a horizontal slit, along with rectangular concrete features.


**Defining the Shapes**

I've got it! The rectangles explain the bunker resemblance. Four distinct rectangles form the basic structure, glued together with a flat, elliptical slab on top. It's a simple, undeniable geometric construction. Now I'm shifting focus to real megalithic dolmens, comparing this structure to Caspar David Friedrich's *Hünengrab im Schnee* to truly grasp the differences in shape and form.


**Revising the Form**

I'm now completely rejecting the rectangular brick analogy. These are NOT bricks; they're glacial boulders! They are irregular, rounded, and weathered, with jagged chips and lichen, not rectangles. These boulders lean, touch at irregular points, and have dirt growing up around them, unlike the "concrete foundation" rectangle I identified earlier. That box needs replacing! And the mine-like shapes? I'm going to rethink the code that spawned those shapes.


**Reimagining the Canvas**

I'm now completely rethinking the approach. The barrow mound itself is the key, and I can sculpt it without resorting to circles or boxes. Using the entire mound from the crest down to y=704, I can achieve continuous surface coverage. The naval mines were visible *because* of circular sky and ground elements – painting the body across the entire mound, plus the mist and horizon across the crest, erases the circles completely and eliminates the bunker aesthetic.


**Refining the Elements**

I'm now focusing on the components that work. The sky remains luminous and peaceful, and the barrow mound's crest evokes the Baltic evening. My next goal is to refine the megalithic tomb; it needs to look like ancient granite, not a concrete bunker. I'll focus on rounding the sharp corners of the stones and weathering the contours with moss and lichen. The chamber should also be a natural, shadowy cave.


**Naturalizing the Components**

The focus is now on replacing the bunker aesthetic with an authentic megalith. My current thought is to eliminate the concrete foundations and transform the upright stones into irregular, weathered glacial boulders. I need them to have jagged edges and crystalline fractures, covered in lichen and moss, deeply embedded in the barrow turf. I'm aiming for an organically natural, ancient look.

events.text:
**Visualizing the Minefield**

I'm now picturing the mine spots as three simultaneous smoke bombs erupting along the ridge. It's a much more dynamic image than I initially conceived; the dust clouds are key, providing a sense of expansion and threat. It makes the battlefield more dangerous and chaotic.


**Analyzing the Board**

I've zeroed in on the absurd bench/bunker combo. That giant brown 2x4 board bolted onto the hill is comedy gold! Each blend call, either for the rectangle (the board) or the ellipses (smoke bombs), behaves exactly as I expect it to -- given my physical understanding of the simulated environment. The rectangle boundaries create sharp lines, and the ellipses form soft, glowing edges. I need to keep this in mind.


**Refining the Techniques**

I'm now zeroing in on painting techniques. I've realized that using `rect(x, y, w, h)` creates sharp-edged cut boxes, and isolated ellipses always leave blobs, which isn't ideal for blending or natural marks. To avoid cut edges, I can blend the entire canvas using `rect(0, 0, 1000, H)`. For the ground, I can use `below(curve)` from x=0 to 1000 all the way to H. I have a new understanding that blending across a full canvas width has no left or right edges. To create natural marks, I need to think in terms of a brush, not a mathematical mask, to achieve soft, feathered edges.


**Concealing the Smoke Bombs**

I'm now thinking about how to effectively hide those smoke bombs. The solution is clear: the barrow mound! If I paint the barrow crest with dark loam across the full width, it will cover the lower half of the smoke, leaving only the sky portions. Adding a horizontal glaze of horizon mist across the same width will neatly obliterate the remaining portion of the puffs. Now, it's about seamlessly blending the layers for that Friedrich feel.


**Transforming the Board**

I'm now completely reimagining the bunker and board as ancient megalithic stones. Instead of the 2x4 and pillbox, I'll be painting a continuous barrow mound with swelling turf. My focus is on eliminating those rectangles; I need to represent stones in an organic way, like the tumulus of the barrow. I'm exploring how oil painters achieve this effect.


**Reimagining the Hünengrab**

Now, I'm analyzing Friedrich's *Hünengrab* paintings. The "board" is gone, completely buried by the barrow mound. I'm focusing on the stones, massive, rounded glacial erratics, not rectangular pillars! The capstone tilts naturally, supported by three rugged boulders. I'm visualizing the dark, shadowed chamber between them and the lichen, all embedded in the heather and peat of the tumulus.


**Considering the Solitude**

I've decided. The landscape is complete and magnificent without any trees! Friedrich's sublime void in works like *Hünengrab* exemplifies this perfectly. The solitary monument, framed by the sky, is a powerful statement. My focus now is on technical execution: ensuring the painting reflects this feeling of quiet solemnity.


**Addressing the Elements**

Now, I'm streamlining the painting. I'm focusing on blending the horizon mist across the full canvas width to erase those smoke bombs completely. Then, I'll bury the 2x4 board with a dark, rich barrow mound spanning the full width, eradicating it from view. Next, I will begin sculpting the stones to their correct, rugged, glacial forms.


**Constructing the Monuments**

I'm now fully immersed in the details. I'm focusing on the capstone: a massive, fractured granite boulder with a silvery sheen. The supporting orthostats will be chunky and rugged, deeply embedded in the barrow. I envision a velvety black cavern between them and will work on ancient lichens. I'm excited about those wind-swept tufts.

-- Chunk 108: Bedding the Dolmen, Painting the Ancient Veteran Oak & Windswept Companion Tree

-- 1. Piles

events.text:
**Observing the Oak Tree**

I'm focused on this image of the oak tree now. The stump is strikingly orange and shaped like a volcanic cinder cone! From the "crater," four sticks radiate outwards, resembling spokes or a satellite dish. One of them extends out to the left like a boom arm. This imagery is quite interesting.


**Analyzing the Artwork**

I'm now deeply considering the essence of sublime art, specifically in the context of Caspar David Friedrich. Focusing on *Der Mönch am Meer* and *Hünengrab*, I see that it is the vastness of the sky, sea, and dunes, coupled with a solitary figure, that creates the masterpiece. My recent attempts to force computer-generated stick trees into the artwork seem misguided, given Friedrich's actual artistic choices. There were no bicycle spokes! I am shifting focus.


**Defining the Sublime Subject**

I'm now zeroing in on the true subject of this artwork: it's the megalithic tomb! Just like *Mondaufgang am Meer*, I am now seeing stones on the shore, the calm Baltic water, the infinite sky, the rising moon, etc. When I take away the superfluous "bicycle spoke" tree, and the right stick, I am seeing a vast glowing German Romantic twilight firmament that is 100% flawless! The waxing crescent moon and evening star really pop in the sky, as does the gentle Baltic coast. But the primary focus is the ancient barrow with the megalithic tomb!


**Refining the Landscape**

I am now envisioning an austere, minimalist landscape like Friedrich's, emphasizing the megalithic tomb's solitude on a Baltic coastal tumulus at dusk, under a silent evening sky with a waxing crescent moon. I'm focusing on incorporating genuine details: glacial erratic boulders, wind-swept grasses, and dried thistle skeletons along the ridge. The goal is to capture the quiet majesty of prehistoric memory and eternity, removing the distracting elements. I am very happy with the direction!


**Eliminating the Distractions**

I've made significant progress by removing the bicycle spokes and right stick, which was an instant improvement. Now, I have a vast twilight sky descending to the barrow's crest, with the orange stump hidden by the mound. The dolmen stands alone, noble and eternal. It's infinitely superior.


**Embracing Romanticism's Essence**

I'm now diving into the core themes of German Romanticism. I've broken down the painting into concrete steps. First, the canvas is completely dry. Next I'll paint the sky, which dominates the scene from the zenith to the horizon, encompassing bands of colors. Then, a rich barrow will emerge, covering the orange stump. It's becoming less abstract and more about capturing the themes of solitude, contemplation, transience, and eternity, in the style of Caspar David Friedrich!


**Constructing the Barrow**

I'm now adding the Megalithic Tomb and glacial erratics, focusing on rugged granite orthostats framing a dark void and a heavy capstone. I'm carefully embedding them into the barrow's turf and placing genuine boulders in the heathland. I'm including windswept grasses, thistle skeletons, and twilight rim-lights for added realism. I'm focusing on the organic textures and natural lighting.

-- Chunk 109: Drying the canvas, restoring the pristine Master Sky, Moon, Star, and Swelling Barrow Mound

-- 1. Dry the canvas completely
wait(2 * 24 * 60)

-- 2. Sky Piles
local p_sky_zenith = pile{{"lead white", 18}, {"cobalt blue", 6.2}, {"smalt", 4.5}, {"raw umber", 0.6}, {"bone black", 0.25}, medium=0.22}
local p_sky_upper  = pile{{"lead white", 26}, {"cobalt blue", 3.2}, {"smalt", 3.2}, {"yellow ochre", 0.8}, {"raw umber", 0.3}, medium=0.22}
local p_sky_mid    = pile{{"lead white", 28}, {"yellow ochre", 3.5}, {"chrome yellow", 0.9}, {"smalt", 1.0}, {"raw umber", 0.2}, {"vermilion", 0.1}, medium=0.22}
local p_sky_glow   = pile{{"lead white", 26}, {"yellow ochre", 5.2}, {"chrome yellow", 2.2}, {"vermilion", 0.5}, {"raw umber", 0.25}, medium=0.22}

-- 3. Four overlapping bands covering x = 0 to 1000 from zenith down behind the barrow (y = 425)
local m1 = rect(0, 0, 1000, 145):soften(30)
work(m1, {hand="body", pile=p_sky_zenith, angle=0, order="across", coverage=2.2, fill=true})

local m2 = rect(0, 105, 1000, 150):soften(30)
work(m2, {hand="body", pile=p_sky_upper, angle=0, order="across", coverage=2.2, fill=true})

local m3 = rect(0, 215, 1000, 140):soften(30)
work(m3, {hand="body", pile=p_sky_mid, angle=0, order="across", coverage=2.2, fill=true})

local m4 = rect(0, 315, 1000, 125):soften(25)
work(m4, {hand="body", pile=p_sky_glow, angle=0, order="across", coverage=2.2, fill=true})

-- 4. Seamless badger blending across the full canvas width
local m_sky_all = rect(0, 0, 1000, 425)
blend(m_sky_all, {angle=1.57})
blend(m_sky_all, {angle=0})

-- 5. Distant low Baltic hills silhouetted in soft atmospheric haze
local p_dist_coast = pile{{"lead white", 15}, {"smalt", 5.0}, {"raw umber", 3.0}, {"red earth", 0.9}, {"bone black", 0.4}, medium=0.25}
local pts_distant_land = {
  {0, 464}, {100, 460}, {220, 454}, {340, 452}, {460, 448},
  {580, 451}, {700, 447}, {820, 452}, {920, 458}, {1000, 464},
  {1000, 475}, {0, 475}
}
local m_coast = poly(pts_distant_land, true):soften(2.5)
work(m_coast, {hand="body", pile=p_dist_coast, angle=0, coverage=1.2, fill=true, clip=true})

-- 6. Calm water sheen and valley mist pooling over the water
local p_water_mist = pile{{"lead white", 26}, {"yellow ochre", 3.2}, {"smalt", 1.8}, {"raw umber", 0.3}, medium=0.3}
local m_water = rect(0, 435, 1000, 30):soften(4)
work(m_water, {hand="glaze", pile=p_water_mist, angle=0, coverage=1.1, fill=false})
blend(rect(0, 432, 1000, 34), {angle=0})

-- 7. Waxing crescent moon and solitary evening star (Venus)
local p_moon_pure = pile{{"lead white", 34}, {"yellow ochre", 1.0}, {"chrome yellow", 0.4}, medium=0.12}
local b_rigger = brush{kind="round", width=1.3, point=1, stiffness=0.85}
b_rigger:load(p_moon_pure, 0.95)
b_rigger:stroke({
  {645.2, 105.5}, {641.5, 108.0}, {639.0, 112.5}, {640.2, 117.0}, {644.0, 119.5}
}, {pressure={0.08, 0.85, 1.0, 0.8, 0.08}, ramps={0.05, 0.05}})

local b_star = brush{kind="round", width=1.0, point=1, stiffness=0.9}
b_star:load(p_moon_pure, 1.0)
b_star:touch(688, 148, {pressure=0.6})

-- 8. The Noble Prehistoric Barrow Mound across Full Lower Canvas
local barrow_nodes = {
  {x=-20, y=465}, {x=80, y=458}, {x=180, y=448}, {x=260, y=430},
  {x=330, y=415}, {x=385, y=408}, {x=445, y=414}, {x=520, y=430},
  {x=600, y=448}, {x=680, y=450}, {x=760, y=436}, {x=830, y=436},
  {x=910, y=448}, {x=1020, y=465}
}

local function barrow_crest(x)
  if x <= barrow_nodes[1].x then return barrow_nodes[1].y end
  if x >= barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].x then return barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].y end
  for i = 1, #barrow_nodes - 1 do
    local p0 = barrow_nodes[i]
    local p1 = barrow_nodes[i+1]
    if x >= p0.x and x <= p1.x then
      local u = (x - p0.x) / (p1.x - p0.x)
      local s = u * u * (3 - 2 * u)
      return p0.y + s * (p1.y - p0.y)
    end
  end
  return 440
end

local m_barrow = below(barrow_crest)

local p_earth_body   = pile{{"raw umber", 10}, {"bone black", 6}, {"red earth", 4}, {"yellow ochre", 3}, medium=0.18}
local p_peat_dark    = pile{{"raw umber", 10}, {"bone black", 7}, {"red earth", 3.5}, medium=0.15}
local p_heath_russet = pile{{"yellow ochre", 6}, {"red earth", 5.5}, {"raw umber", 5}, {"lead white", 2}, medium=0.2}

-- Solid body fill across the entire barrow from crest to bottom (covers the tree stump completely!)
work(m_barrow, {
  hand = "body",
  pile = p_earth_body,
  angle = 0.22,
  length = {50, 110},
  coverage = 2.4,
  fill = true,
  clip = true
})

-- Summit heather bank
local m_summit = (ellipse(385, 435, 170, 32) + ellipse(250, 448, 140, 35)):soften(15) * m_barrow
work(m_summit, {hand="body", pile=p_heath_russet, angle=0.18, coverage=1.4, fill=true})

-- Blend barrow smoothly (no horizontal cutoffs!)
blend(m_barrow, {angle=0.2})
blend(m_barrow, {angle=-0.15})

-- Firm, organic stroke along the natural barrow crest against the glowing mist
local b_crest = brush{kind="round", width=2.8, point=1, stiffness=0.9}
b_crest:load(p_peat_dark, 0.95)
local crest_line = {}
for x = -10, 1010, 10 do

- day 32, 07:23: Returning to the easel to critically evaluate the canvas. The painting left from previous sessions suffered from acute structural and aesthetic flaws: awkward stick-figure branches, artificial geometric polygons, cut rectangular blend boundaries, and an unintegrated foreground.
Guided by Friedrich's authentic methodology and materials, we embarked on a complete, uncompromising transformation of the work:
1. ### *Hünengrab im Abendlicht* (Megalithic Tomb in Evening Light)

An ancient prehistoric dolmen crowns the summit of a desolate Baltic coastal barrow (*Hünengrab*) in late autumn twilight. Prepared on a handwoven linen support with a warm knife-leveled ground and brushed lead-white surface, the landscape rises into an immense, luminous firmament that gradates from a pale amber afterglow at the horizon through silvery-buff twilight into a deep, serene cobalt and smalt blue at the zenith. In the quiet upper sky, the slender waxing crescent moon and the solitary evening star (*Hesperus*) shine serenely.

Beyond the dark, rolling ridge of the burial mound, cool evening mist pools over quiet coastal waters, with low distant headlands silhouetted against the afterglow. The megalithic tomb—two massive, rugged orthostats of Scandinavian glacial erratic granite supporting an angular, weathered capstone encrusted with pale sage and golden crustose lichen—frames a sacred, pitch-black chamber void that contemplates the passage of millennia, human mortality, and the eternal silence of the Baltic dusk. Along the crest of the tumulus, delicate bent-grass tufts and dried carline thistle skeletons sway softly in the coastal wind.

events.text:
**Analyzing Tree Overpainting**

I've been reviewing chunks 108 and 109 and found an interesting progression. It seems someone initially painted an oak and its companion tree in chunk 108. Then, in chunk 109, they decided to completely repaint those trees, but this time with the sky. I'm focusing on the change in aesthetic.


**Investigating Blending Techniques**

I'm now diving into the implications of the "soften" command and how it influenced the final look of the sky. The initial application used multiple soft-edged rectangles, followed by a blend across the whole sky area. The studio notes on light application over wet dark are relevant because, when the trees were painted, the paint was dry or tack-dry. In chunk 109, they applied body paint with coverage=2, after waiting, suggesting a deliberate layering strategy.


**Examining Hidden Features**

I'm now zeroing in on the overpainting of the branches and trunk, specifically focusing on the visible remnants of the earlier oak tree in chunks 108 and 109. I've pinpointed dark marks that correspond precisely with the twigs from the previous version, even after the sky layers. I'm also seeing a ghost of the companion tree trunk. This suggests a careful attempt to cover but not completely obliterate the initial composition.


**Considering Oak Tree Symbolism**

I'm now drawing parallels between the oak tree's depiction on our canvas and the recurring imagery in Caspar David Friedrich's work. The solitary tree, the twisted branches, the association with ancient sites – these all resonate with themes of contemplation, mortality, and the sublime. I'm noting the dolmen's placement and how it echoes the motif of ancient, monumental forms. I'm exploring how the oak embodies these concepts within this landscape.


**Interpreting Artistic Abandonment**

I'm now grappling with the artist's apparent frustration. The latest canvas iteration is stark: a barren mud hill under a bleak sky. There are no trees at all! The dolmen is simple and uninspired, and the sky is marked with dirty flecks. The artist repeatedly failed with trees, giving up and claiming completion, which is curious given the other revisions in earlier chunks. The journal entry reveals a struggle with branch depiction, leading to an abrupt, almost defeated, conclusion.


**Exploring Friedrich's Techniques**

I'm now focusing on how the latest landscape rendition fails to capture Friedrich's essence. The focus shifts from merely mimicking his style to understanding the deeper principles that make his work powerful. Considering the brief and studio rules, I see now I need to engage directly with Friedrich's *Quercus robur* and architectural landscape elements, which I was not doing before. My current canvas lacks the sacred presence of nature, instead settling for a crude imitation.


**Describing the Ancient Oak**

I am now visualizing the key elements: the ancient trunk with its deep furrows and root buttresses. I am considering the stark, skeletal crown against the cold sky, and the muscular, living limbs that protect the megalithic tomb. The authentic oak branching and sparse, late-autumn leaves are also in sharp focus. I'm exploring how these details can portray the sculpture of time and survival. The companion oak is on my radar as well.


**Visualizing Megalithic Burial Mounds**

I'm currently focused on the dolmen's authenticity, contrasting the current flat capstone with the reality of colossal glacial erratics in the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern region, where Friedrich grew up. The "ironing board" effect and uniform gray brushwork are not remotely representative. I'm noting the irregular facets, crystalline surfaces, and lichen-covered stones, particularly the reddish-gray granites. The vertical orthostats are vague slabs, whereas I am now focused on the irregular facets of actual Hünengräber stones. The pitch-black chamber below the dolmen is also a key element.


**Depicting Baltic Heathland**

I'm now zeroing in on the Baltic heathland elements. I'm focusing on the undulating banks of heather and deep peat, contrasting with the golden-russet grasses. I'm particularly interested in how weathered glacial stones and the silhouettes of carline thistle can be incorporated. My goal is to capture the windswept feeling of late autumn dusk, with a subtle path leading the eye.

**Analyzing the Visual Evidence**

I've just examined chunks 108 and 109 closely. Chunk 108 shows a painted tree with bold strokes on the bole and limbs. Chunk 109 shows restoration of the sky. I can tell the sky was covered, and then uncovered. My current analysis focuses on discerning the reason for the covering.


**Considering the Abandonment**

I'm now contemplating the shift in artistic direction. The initial focus was on a landscape including trees, but the subsequent chunks reveal an abandonment of that vision in favor of the dolmen on a knoll. The sky was covered, then re-rendered, and then the sky details were elaborated to reflect the time the painting would be "set." It's odd that the sky was painted over! I'm now critically examining the quality of the dolmen rendering in the final version.


**Evaluating the Artifact's Quality**

I'm now very concerned about the quality of the final dolmen rendering. The uprights appear cartoonish, like gray pillars or tiles, with a dark brown square between them, and curved highlights. The sky exhibits black dashes and scratch marks that are remnants of the tree twigs, along with blotches and floating lines. The foreground mound is a bland brown blob. The composition feels empty and unbalanced. The work bears no resemblance to Friedrich.


**Revisiting Oak Trees**

I'm now consumed with the crucial need to capture majestic oak trees in the style of Caspar David Friedrich. My initial frustration stems from previous, unsatisfactory attempts at branch rendering. I must avoid the fatal error of single-stroke lines that create rubbery splines, and think sympodial branches. The essence of Friedrich's dolmen paintings is the oaks, but previous attempts failed!


**Analyzing Branch Structure**

I'm now focusing on branch structure. I'm noting the need for angular segments and the critical importance of knotty joints and tapering. I'm recalling the use of "b_limb" and "b_branch" in the Lua code, which seemed too simple to handle this. I am now considering parallel vertical strokes for trunks - leading to gaps. I have refreshed my notes and am now exploring acrotony, sympodial branching, and the branch-area rule, particularly the side branch thickness issue. I am also now considering the ancient oaks retrenching!

events.text:
Returning to the easel to critically evaluate the canvas and bring the work to its true Friedrichian culmination.
Close inspection of the canvas reveals several crucial issues that must be addressed:
1. Composition and Soul: The painting currently lacks its most essential Caspar David Friedrich elements—the monumental ancient bare oak tree and its companion. Without the ancient, gnarled veteran oak sheltering the prehistoric tomb and spearing into the twilight sky, the composition feels vacant and disconnected from the profound dialogue between mortal history, nature, and cosmic eternity.
2. Sky Firmament: While the moon and evening star shine quietly in the upper sky, the mid-sky retains stray ghost ticks and marks from earlier underpaintings that need soft veil integration.
3. The Megalithic Tomb (Hünengrab): The current stone structure appears somewhat flat and pillbox-like, lacking the authentic crystalline fracture facets, heavy mass, and weathered Scandinavian granite character of Baltic glacial erratics (Findlinge).
4. Foreground Heathland: The burial mound requires rich topography and authentic late-autumn Baltic heathland texture—undulating heather banks (Calluna vulgaris), mossy turf folds, half-buried glacial stones, a worn pilgrim path, and crisp carline thistle silhouettes.

Plan of work:
Phase 1: Perfect the twilight sky and atmosphere, softly veiling stray sky marks with luminous body color and refining the low Baltic horizon mist and distant headland.
Phase 2: Sculpt the Megalithic Tomb into an authentic, monumental Scandinavian granite dolmen with crystalline cleavage planes, weathered texture, deep cavern void, and crustose lichens.
Phase 3: Construct the majestic Ancient Veteran Oak (Quercus robur) to the left of the dolmen—its hollowed, furrowed trunk with flaring root buttresses, its retrenched bleached stag-antlers reaching into the cobalt zenith, and its muscular living bough arching over the tomb with sympodial branching and delicate clinging marcescent leaves.

I'm now zeroing in on the capstone, specifically look-0138. The silhouette still resembles a rounded dome, like a large saucer. The front facet is peculiar, with a sharp horizontal cut through an odd polygon band, which is something I need to understand better.

I'm now deep-diving into the visual details. The uprights present as flat pillars framing a black doorway. The side stones are sharp polygons. I've spotted two black diagonal dashed lines in the sky above the capstone, and those coordinates, those black marks above the capstone, suggest an explanation for the saucer/dome appearance.


**Clarifying the Scene**

I've made a breakthrough. The tomb isn't some flat bunker; it's a rough, irregular boulder resting on others, flanked by three enormous ancient oak trees. The trees are the key! Their branches create those black lines in the image, adding the necessary scale and atmosphere. Without them, the dolmen lacks any poetic weight. The oak trunks, specifically, were at x ≈ 270, and its branches arched right over the dolmen at y ≈ 300 to 350, providing the visual context!


**Revisiting the Composition**

I realize the artist erased the oak tree, leaving its branch marks floating. The companion tree trunk was on the right at x ≈ 750-880. I'm focusing on the dolmen's realism: the capstone's silhouette must be irregular, with asymmetrical fractures; the orthostats, uneven; the shadow, a broken recess; and the capstone's texture and tones, weathered. The composition hinges on these corrections.


**Refining the Trees**

I'm now detailing the oak trees, confirming their placement. The main tree's eastern limb arches over the dolmen, encompassing the floating marks. Its western limb extends left, while its upper crown has died back, spearing the sky. The companion tree on the right will encompass those marks at x ≈ 750-880. I'm also considering the open sky: the space between the trees for the moon and stars, from x = 500 to 720.


**Pinpointing the Style**

I now understand the visual anomaly. The use of `clip=true` with the polygonal definition of the dolmen's elements, specifically in look-0138, created that unnatural, low-poly appearance. The sharp straight lines and clipped fills reproduced the outlines precisely, giving it the 3D polygonal model feel. The dolmen, now, must be rendered with more organic, rugged features to fix this artistic error. I also need to focus on the sky to give a classic Caspar David Friedrich impression: (645, 112) and the evening star at (688, 148)! **Understanding the Error**

I'm now focused on painting the dolmen using traditional brushstrokes. I'm visualizing the brush's texture on the capstone, specifically the western side's shoulder and chipped corner. **Analyzing Visual Patterns**

I'm focusing intently on look-0144 and look-0145. I've noted a distinct visual characteristic: the tree's form appears as straight wooden segments connected at sharp angles. This is crucial; I need to understand why this visual characteristic exists. I need to dissect the nature of these observations. This feels critical to understanding the bigger picture.


**Deconstructing the Geometry**

I've zeroed in on the geometrical underpinnings. The trunk's a polygon with concave curves; the hollow, a black pill. The bough abruptly changes direction, ending with a flat line. I'm seeing straight triangular wedges as branches. Stag antlers are also flat sticks, with sharp lines. This matches prior observations about stick-figure branches. I'm digging into `easel_guide.md` and `trees.md` to see how organic forms are created, seeking solutions by looking at drawing styles.


**Exploring Brushstrokes and Styles**

I'm now deep-diving into the nuances of brushstrokes, especially how they might mimic natural forms. I am exploring how `body_of` can be used. The function seems to create the silhouette of a skeleton using points and widths. Now I am trying to understand how a human painter would actually depict a tree. I now see it's about using the right brush: a pointed round, a rigger, or a filbert.


**Understanding Brush Dynamics**

I'm now focused on replicating the painter's technique to understand how the organic forms can be created. I'm seeing that branches are drawn with continuous, tapered strokes. Pressure reduction from base to tip creates a smooth taper, while the hand's natural movements introduce organic curvature. I am also investigating why a polygon was used instead of brushstrokes and the implications of this. I am now trying to compare and contrast the different approaches.


**Testing the Techniques**

I'm getting excited: I can now test the painter's method I identified. Using specific brush parameters, I generated tapered branches, and they look natural! I am testing the new technique on a geometric polygon tree, and now realize how composition impacts the design of the tree. The location of the tree transforms the whole scene!


**Defining the Organic Elements**

I'm now zeroing in on Friedrich's oaks and their key characteristics. The goal is to make my tree truly resemble an authentic, organic, gnarled oak. I've realized that the tree needs to have a gnarled, weathered trunk with muscular root flares. The hollow is an irregular, organic split in the wood with thick, rounded wound-wood lips that have grown over centuries. Additionally, the stag-headed dead crown needs to be jagged, splintered, and fractured. Lightning or rot broke the top trunk, so the structure should reflect that.


**Visualizing the Tree's Anatomy**

I'm now picturing the tree's final form, starting with the dead top. It has jagged, fractured stubs with zigzagging, bleached antlers. The living eastern bough is a powerful, muscular curve, with gnarled elbows and knobby burls, while the western bough balances the tree. The winter foliage is delicate, with russet and amber leaves. I now have a clearer mental image of how the artist creates the form.


**Testing Brush Applications**

I am now experimenting with brush applications. I'm focusing on creating organic, tapering branches. I've been studying the `easel_guide.md` file and learned that a pointed round brush with pressure variations allows for precise control of stroke width. I've noted that pressure gradients, combined with curved splines, create authentic, hand-drawn effects. Now, I'm working to apply these techniques to develop the proper width of the trunk and limbs. I'm measuring trunk width and root flares.


**Applying Brushwork Solutions**

I'm now implementing the painting solutions to create the organic tree trunk and bough. I'm focusing on the details: the root flare reaches approximately x=305, y=452, with the trunk varying in width. I'm planning to use overlapping vertical strokes with a wide filbert brush to build up a solid, opaque trunk. The bough, starting at (278, 362), will be painted with a similar approach, employing a graceful arching curve and pressure variation for a tapered effect.


**Implementing Branch Structure**

I'm now focused on fleshing out the tree's secondary branches, specifically the eastern and western boughs. I've defined three branches for the eastern bough and two for the western, including stroke positions and pressure values to define tapered effects. I am also working to remove the straight sticks that form the stag-head crown in look-0144. I now need to determine how to create a jagged, fractured crown.


**Refining the Antlers**

I'm now zeroing in on the stag-antlers. My focus is on completely removing those straight sticks from look-0144 by painting over the sky. I plan to use a smooth sky passage from the zenith color down to the upper sky to erase the offending sticks. I'm going to then paint authentic, gnarled antlers over the clean sky, and now have a new plan for the dolmen.

-- 2. Define the skyline contour: down to the capstone top at dolmen (y ≈ 376), and barrow crest elsewhere
local barrow_nodes = {
  {x=-20, y=465}, {x=80, y=458}, {x=180, y=448}, {x=260, y=430},
  {x=315, y=390}, {x=350, y=376}, {x=395, y=375}, {x=440, y=377},

  {x=760, y=436}, {x=830, y=436}, {x=910, y=448}, {x=1020, y=465}
}

local function skyline(x)
  if x <= barrow_nodes[1].x then return barrow_nodes[1].y end
  if x >= barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].x then return barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].y end
  for i = 1, #barrow_nodes - 1 do
    local p0 = barrow_nodes[i]
    local p1 = barrow_nodes[i+1]
    if x >= p0.x and x <= p1.x then

      local s = u * u * (3 - 2 * u)
      return p0.y + s * (p1.y - p0.y)
    end
  end
  return 430
end

The coordinates confirm it: look-0151 is a post-and-lintel shed, not a dolmen. The horizontal capstone rests atop two vertical columns with a doorway between them. It is not like a real megalithic dolmen in Friedrich's art or Baltic archaeology, which are piles of irregular glacial boulders. It's a structure with flat walls and a roof, unlike the chunky, irregular shapes I would expect.


**Refining the Composition**

I'm now zeroing in on the composition. I need to eliminate the "garage door" and incorporate the angular Scandinavian granite rock, which sits atop leaning boulders. The presence of ancient oaks is essential. In *Hünengrab im Schnee*, the oak trunks frame the scene, breaking the silhouette. Also, I need to reshape the beige path, now a driveway, into a more natural ascent.


**Revising the Design**

I'm now fully immersed in refining the design. The "doorway" must become dark, mysterious crevices between boulders, eliminating any sense of a square opening. The orthostats will be rugged, rounded glacial boulders, not flat walls, and the capstone will be similarly irregular and weathered. The path is gone! I am now painting over the path with rolling banks of dark vegetation.


**Incorporating the Details**

I'm now integrating heather and peat to transform the barrow into a desolate burial mound, capturing the romantic solitude of Friedrich's spirit. The Veteran Stag-Headed Oak on the left and the Windswept Companion Oak on the right are crucial. I'm placing the Ancient Oak at x ≈ 250 to 285, its gnarled trunk rising next to the stones, its bough arching over the tomb, and its stag-antlers reaching into the twilight sky. -- 2. Define the Natural Swelling Barrow Crest
local barrow_nodes = {
  {x=-20, y=465}, {x=80, y=458}, {x=180, y=448}, {x=260, y=430},
  {x=330, y=415}, {x=385, y=408}, {x=445, y=414}, {x=520, y=430},
  {x=600, y=448}, {x=680, y=450}, {x=760, y=436}, {x=830, y=436},
  {x=910, y=448}, {x=1020, y=465}
}

local function barrow_crest(x)
  if x <= barrow_nodes[1].x then return barrow_nodes[1].y end
  if x >= barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].x then return barrow_nodes[#barrow_nodes].y end
  for i = 1, #barrow_nodes - 1 do
    local p0 = barrow_nodes[i]
    local p1 = barrow_nodes[i+1]
    if x >= p0.x and x <= p1.x then
      local u = (x - p0.x) / (p1.x - p0.x)
      local s = u * u * (3 - 2 * u)
      return p0.y + s * (p1.y - p0.y)
    end
  end
  return 430
end

**Analyzing the Dolmen**

I'm focusing intently on this dolmen, impressed by its natural scale and authentic, heroic presence atop the tumulus. The prehistoric stone cairn is now complete, and the pale ring from the previous sky pass around its base is noteworthy. It all feels natural.


**Adding the Trees**

I'm now consumed with adding the trees. The great oak, *Quercus robur*, will be rooted into the barrow's slope, its buttresses reaching toward the dolmen. Across the misty valley, I'm envisioning a windswept companion tree to balance the scene. I am now deep into the detail of the roots and the ancient hollow trunk of the great oak, working out its placement and form with care and precision, to ensure they provide a majestic foreground.


**Detailing the Bough**

I'm now deep in the meticulous detail of the oak's eastern bough. The trunk's split and the swell of the branch collar at (275, 355) is coming to life. I've mapped the arching trajectory across the sky, noting its graceful taper. I'm carefully determining the exact point the limb passes over the capstone and considering the secondary branches that spring from it. Now I am defining the bark texture of the trunk and the ancient hollow.


**Defining the Twigs**

I'm now intricately defining the secondary branches and twigs, meticulously noting each start and end point. I'm focusing on the subtle arches and droops. The living western bough is taking shape, and the sympodial twigs are branching at the nodes of the eastern boughs, with care and precision, including swelling branch collars at every branch point.


**Constructing the Crown**

I'm now consumed by the "Die Totenkrone." The dead trunk rises from (268, 355) towards the zenith. I'm focusing on the weathered umber and bone-gray wood, and meticulously crafting the antler-like branches, plotting their precise trajectories across the canvas. I'm carefully depicting the splintered tips that pierce the cobalt sky, feeling a visceral connection to the scene.


**Positioning the Oak**

I am now focusing on the positioning of a storm-twisted oak. I've placed its roots on the crest of the right knoll. I'm carefully charting the trunk's rise from (760, 436), through (756, 400), (752, 365), (748, 330), and (745, 295). I've planned the eastward sweep of the branches, noting their coordinates and trajectories, defining boughs C1, C2, and C3. I am picturing the crooked twigs and sparse leaves.

**Deepening the Ground**

I'm now consumed by deepening the ground. I'm focusing on bedding the dolmen and tree roots into dark peat and heather. I'm adding windswept bent-grass plumes and dried carline thistle skeletons. I'm now contemplating how to render the trees with a rich, solid, organic look, void of polygon artifacts, using studio tools.


**Crafting the Wood**

I'm now implementing a new workflow. I'm using `poly(pts, true)` filled with `work()` to build a solid base for the trunk and limbs, ensuring full opacity and no streaking. I'm then layering longitudinal furrows and raised bark ridges with pointed brushes to create texture. Hollow cavities are filled with rounded wound-wood calluses. For main limbs, I'm employing `ribbon(pts, widths)` for smoothly tapered forms.

-- Construct the Monumental Ancient Veteran Oak, Companion Tree, and Heath Accents

-- 1. Pigment Piles

local p_hollow_void = pile{{"bone black", 16}, {"raw umber", 6}, medium=0.1}

local p_stag_dark   = pile{{"bone black", 8}, {"raw umber", 8}, {"lead white", 4}, {"smalt", 1.5}, medium=0.16}
local p_stag_bleach = pile{{"lead white", 18}, {"raw umber", 4.5}, {"yellow ochre", 2.5}, {"smalt", 1.5}, medium=0.18}
local p_stag_tip    = pile{{"lead white", 24}, {"raw umber", 3.0}, {"yellow ochre", 2.0}, {"smalt", 1.2}, medium=0.18}

local p_leaf_russet = pile{{"red earth", 7}, {"yellow ochre", 6}, {"raw umber", 5}, {"lead white", 2}, medium=0.2}
local p_leaf_gold   = pile{{"yellow ochre", 11}, {"chrome yellow", 2.5}, {"red earth", 2.5}, {"lead white", 3}, medium=0.22}
local p_leaf_rim    = pile{{"lead white", 14}, {"yellow ochre", 10}, {"chrome yellow", 3.0}, medium=0.2}

local p_peat_dark    = pile{{"raw umber", 11}, {"bone black", 8}, {"red earth", 3.5}, medium=0.15}
local p_heather_purp = pile{{"raw umber", 7}, {"red earth", 6.0}, {"bone black", 3.5}, {"smalt", 2.0}, medium=0.18}
local p_straw_sharp  = pile{{"lead white", 18}, {"yellow ochre", 9}, {"chrome yellow", 1.2}, {"raw umber", 1.0}, medium=0.22}
local p_straw_shade  = pile{{"yellow ochre", 7}, {"raw umber", 6}, {"bone black", 2.5}, {"lead white", 2.0}, medium=0.2}

local b_block  = brush{kind="filbert", width=7.0, stiffness=0.85}
local b_branch = brush{kind="round", width=3.2, point=1, stiffness=0.85}
local b_twig   = brush{kind="round", width=1.4, point=1, stiffness=0.9}
local b_rigger = brush{kind="round", width=0.8, point=1, stiffness=0.9}

-- 2. Bed the Dolmen Base into Tumulus Peat & Heather
b_block:load(p_peat_dark, 0.95)
b_block:stroke({{320, 416}, {355, 418}, {385, 420}, {415, 419}, {445, 416}}, {pressure=0.95})
b_block:load(p_heather_purp, 0.95)
b_block:stroke({{325, 418}, {360, 420}, {390, 421}, {420, 420}, {440, 418}}, {pressure=0.9})

-- 3. The Ancient Veteran Oak: Solid Trunk Bole & Root Buttresses
-- Define smoothed organic trunk contour (width ~26 to 34)
local pts_trunk = {
  {238, 452}, {248, 436}, {256, 415}, {260, 390}, {262, 365},
  {270, 355}, {278, 355}, {284, 368}, {282, 392}, {284, 415},
  {295, 434}, {315, 446}, {300, 454}, {278, 452}, {255, 454}
}
local m_trunk = poly(pts_trunk, true)
work(m_trunk, {hand="body", pile=p_bark_core, angle=1.5, coverage=2.5, fill=true, clip=true})

-- Deep longitudinal bark furrows
b_twig:load(p_bark_furrow, 0.95)
b_twig:stroke({{264, 362}, {262, 390}, {258, 418}, {250, 444}}, {pressure={0.8, 0.9, 0.8, 0.3}})
b_twig:stroke({{271, 360}, {270, 390}, {268, 418}, {264, 448}}, {pressure={0.8, 0.9, 0.8, 0.4}})
b_twig:stroke({{278, 365}, {278, 392}, {277, 418}, {280, 448}}, {pressure={0.8, 0.9, 0.8, 0.4}})
b_twig:stroke({{282, 380}, {283, 408}, {290, 432}, {306, 446}}, {pressure={0.7, 0.85, 0.8, 0.3}})

-- Raised weathered bark ridges
b_twig:load(p_bark_mid, 0.9)
b_twig:stroke({{266, 362}, {264, 390}, {260, 416}, {254, 442}}, {pressure={0.5, 0.75, 0.7, 0.2}})
b_twig:stroke({{274, 362}, {274, 390}, {272, 416}, {272, 446}}, {pressure={0.5, 0.75, 0.7, 0.2}})
b_twig:stroke({{280, 372}, {281, 400}, {284, 424}, {298, 444}}, {pressure={0.5, 0.75, 0.7, 0.2}})

-- Highlights along crest of bark ridges
b_rigger:load(p_bark_ridge, 0.85)
b_rigger:stroke({{266, 375}, {265, 400}, {261, 424}}, {pressure={0.3, 0.65, 0.2}})
b_rigger:stroke({{275, 375}, {275, 400}, {273, 424}}, {pressure={0.3, 0.65, 0.2}})

-- Ancient hollow cavity in trunk (x = 267 to 275, y = 396 to 424)

work(m_hollow, {hand="detail", pile=p_hollow_void, angle=1.5, coverage=2.2, fill=true, clip=true})

-- Wound-wood calluses framing the hollow
b_twig:load(p_woundwood, 0.9)

-- Bark light along crest of eastern bough

  {pressure={0.7, 0.75, 0.7, 0.65, 0.5, 0.25}, ramps={0.02, 0.05}})

-- Swelling branch collar at trunk junction
b_block:load(p_bark_core, 0.95)

-- Secondary Branches off Eastern Bough:
-- E1 (above left of dolmen): arches upward into twilight
local pts_e1 = {
  {342, 340}, {360, 318}, {378, 292}, {395, 268},
  {399, 270}, {383, 294}, {365, 321}, {347, 342}
}
work(poly(pts_e1, true), {hand="body", pile=p_bark_core, angle=1.0, coverage=2.2, fill=true, clip=true})
b_twig:load(p_bark_mid, 0.85)
b_twig:stroke({{344, 339}, {362, 318}, {380, 292}, {397, 268}}, {pressure={0.6, 0.65, 0.45, 0.15}})

-- E2 (above right of dolmen): arches upward and eastward

  {474, 266}, {457, 286}, {435, 311}, {413, 334}

work(poly(pts_e2, true), {hand="body", pile=p_bark_core, angle=0.8, coverage=2.2, fill=true, clip=true})
b_twig:load(p_bark_mid, 0.85)
b_twig:stroke({{410, 331}, {432, 308}, {454, 284}, {472, 264}}, {pressure={0.55, 0.6, 0.45, 0.15}})

-- E3 (drooping shelter east of dolmen):
b_branch:load(p_bark_core, 0.95)
b_branch:stroke({{450, 328}, {475, 338}, {498, 348}, {518, 355}}, {pressure={0.85, 0.7, 0.45, 0.15}, ramps={0.02, 0.1}})

-- 5. The Living Western Bough (Reaching out over descending left knoll)
local pts_west_bough = {
  {262, 356}, {225, 345}, {185, 332}, {145, 316}, {118, 300},
  {118, 308}, {145, 324}, {185, 340}, {225, 354}, {260, 366}
}
local m_west_bough = poly(pts_west_bough, true)
work(m_west_bough, {hand="body", pile=p_bark_core, angle=-0.15, coverage=2.4, fill=true, clip=true})

b_twig:load(p_bark_mid, 0.9)
b_twig:stroke({{260, 357}, {225, 346}, {185, 333}, {145, 317}, {118, 302}},
  {pressure={0.7, 0.75, 0.65, 0.5, 0.2}, ramps={0.02, 0.05}})

-- Western collar
b_block:load(p_bark_core, 0.95)
b_block:stroke({{264, 356}, {258, 362}, {260, 370}}, {pressure=0.9})

-- Secondary Western Limbs:
-- W1 (upward reaching toward zenith west)
local pts_w1 = {

work(poly(pts_w1, true), {hand="body", pile=p_bark_core, angle=-1.1, coverage=2.2, fill=true, clip=true})

local pts_stag_center = {

}
local m_stag_center = poly(pts_stag_center, true)
work(m_stag_center, {hand="body", pile=p_stag_dark, angle=1.55, coverage=2.4, fill=true, clip=true})

-- Bleached bone-gray highlights along dead trunk
b_twig:load(p_stag_bleach, 0.95)
b_twig:stroke({{268, 355}, {266, 310}, {263, 265}, {260, 215}, {257, 165}, {254, 128}},

b_rigger:stroke({{254, 130}, {253, 118}}, {pressure={0.45, 0.05}})
b_rigger:stroke({{254, 130}, {257, 120}}, {pressure={0.35, 0.05}})
b_rigger:stroke({{254, 130}, {250, 122}}, {pressure={0.3, 0.05}})

local pts_antler_e = {

  {335, 141}, {323, 180}, {307, 218}, {288, 257}, {270, 294}

work(poly(pts_antler_e, true), {hand="detail", pile=p_stag_dark, angle=0.9, coverage=2.2, fill=true, clip=true})
b_twig:load(p_stag_bleach, 0.95)
b_twig:stroke({{268, 292}, {286, 255}, {306, 216}, {322, 178}, {334, 139}},
  {pressure={0.5, 0.7, 0.6, 0.4, 0.1}, ramps={0.02, 0.05}})
b_rigger:load(p_stag_tip, 1.0)
b_rigger:stroke({{334, 141}, {338, 128}}, {pressure={0.4, 0.05}})
b_rigger:stroke({{334, 141}, {332, 130}}, {pressure={0.3, 0.05}})

-- Antler Branch S2 (West Stag Antler)
local pts_antler_w = {
  {263, 282}, {245, 245}, {226, 206}, {208, 168}, {194, 132},
  {197, 131}, {211, 167}, {229, 204}, {248, 243}, {266, 280}
}
work(poly(pts_antler_w, true), {hand="detail", pile=p_stag_dark, angle=-0.9, coverage=2.2, fill=true, clip=true})
b_twig:load(p_stag_bleach, 0.95)
b_twig:stroke({{264, 281}, {246, 244}, {227, 205}, {209, 167}, {195, 130}},
  {pressure={0.5, 0.7, 0.6, 0.4, 0.1}, ramps={0.02, 0.05}})
b_rigger:load(p_stag_tip, 1.0)
b_rigger:stroke({{195, 132}, {192, 122}}, {pressure={0.4, 0.05}})
b_rigger:stroke({{195, 132}, {197, 124}}, {pressure={0.3, 0.05}})

-- 7. Sympodial Crooked Oak Twigs
local oak_twigs = {
  -- Off E1
  {{397, 268}, {408, 250}, {418, 234}},
  {{397, 268}, {390, 248}, {384, 232}},
  {{380, 292}, {370, 272}, {362, 254}},
  {{362, 318}, {352, 298}, {346, 282}},
  -- Off E2
  {{472, 264}, {484, 246}, {496, 230}},
  {{472, 264}, {464, 244}, {458, 226}},
  {{454, 284}, {466, 266}, {476, 250}},
  -- Off E3
  {{498, 348}, {514, 360}, {528, 370}},
  {{518, 355}, {534, 352}, {550, 348}},
  -- Off W1
  {{142, 251}, {130, 232}, {120, 216}},
  {{142, 251}, {150, 230}, {156, 212}},
  {{157, 279}, {146, 260}, {136, 242}},
  {{174, 309}, {164, 290}, {156, 272}},
  -- Off W2
  {{125, 338}, {110, 352}, {96, 364}},
  {{104, 352}, {90, 346}, {76, 340}}
}
for _, tw in ipairs(oak_twigs) do
  b_twig:load(p_bark_core, 0.9)
  b_twig:stroke(tw, {pressure={0.75, 0.2}, ramps={0.02, 0.15}})

-- Fine outer sympodial twigs
local fine_twigs = {
  {{418, 234}, {426, 222}, {432, 212}},
  {{384, 232}, {378, 218}, {374, 206}},
  {{496, 230}, {506, 218}, {514, 206}},
  {{476, 250}, {486, 236}, {494, 224}},
  {{120, 216}, {112, 204}, {106, 194}},

}

  b_rigger:load(p_bark_core, 0.85)
  b_rigger:stroke(ftw, {pressure={0.65, 0.1}, ramps={0.02, 0.15}})

-- 8. Ragged Marcescent Late-Autumn Oak Foliage

  {405, 252, 14}, {385, 278, 12}, {362, 308, 14}, {348, 292, 10},
  {468, 272, 14}, {452, 296, 12}, {492, 238, 12}, {478, 258, 10},

  {178, 320, 14}, {158, 292, 12}, {142, 262, 14}, {128, 238, 12},

    b_rigger:touch(cx + ox, cy + oy, {pressure=rand(0.25, 0.5), drag={1.0, 1.2}})

}

end

-- Sparse clinging leaves on companion tree
local comp_leaf_sprays = {
  {810, 300, 12}, {840, 280, 14}, {865, 265, 12}, {828, 250, 12},
  {775, 240, 12}, {785, 210, 10}
}
for _, cl in ipairs(comp_leaf_sprays) do
  local cx, cy, n = cl[1], cl[2], cl[3]
  for i = 1, n do
    local ox = rand(-10, 10)
    local oy = rand(-8, 8)
    local p = (rand(0, 1) < 0.5) and p_leaf_russet or p_leaf_gold
    b_leaf:load(p, 0.7)
    b_leaf:touch(cx + ox, cy + oy, {pressure=rand(0.3, 0.65), drag={rand(1.0, 2.0), 1.4}})
  end
end

-- 10. Windswept Bent-Grass Tufts & Dried Carline Thistles along Crest
local function draw_curved_grass(bx, by, len, ang, bend, p)
  local mx = bx + len * 0.55 * math.cos(ang + bend * 0.5)
  local my = by - len * 0.55 * math.sin(ang + bend * 0.5)
  local tx = bx + len * math.cos(ang + bend)
  local ty = by - len * math.sin(ang + bend)
  b_rigger:load(p, 0.75)
  b_rigger:stroke({{bx, by}, {mx, my}, {tx, ty}}, {pressure={0.6, 0.04}, ramps={0.05, 0.3}})
end

local function draw_grass_cluster(cx, cy, n, h, lean)
  for i = 1, n do
    local bx = cx + rand(-5, 5)
    local by = cy + rand(-2, 2)
    local len = h * rand(0.75, 1.25)
    local ang = 1.57 + rand(-0.25, 0.25) + lean * 0.3
    local bnd = lean * rand(0.2, 0.5)
    local p = (rand(0, 1) < 0.65) and p_straw_sharp or p_straw_shade
    draw_curved_grass(bx, by, len, ang, bnd, p)
  end
end

local crest_grasses = {
  {160, 448, 8, 16, -0.35}, {210, 438, 7, 14, -0.3},
  {310, 416, 7, 13, -0.2},  {435, 415, 7, 13, 0.2},
  {480, 422, 8, 15, 0.25},  {530, 432, 8, 15, 0.3},
  {630, 448, 7, 14, 0.3},   {720, 440, 8, 16, 0.35},
  {810, 436, 8, 15, 0.35},  {890, 446, 7, 14, 0.4}
}
for _, g in ipairs(crest_grasses) do
  draw_grass_cluster(g[1], g[2], g[3], g[4], g[5])
end

-- Dried carline thistle skeletons (Carlina vulgaris) silhouetted against glowing mist
local thistles = {
  {180, 448, 18}, {230, 435, 16}, {510, 428, 17}, {610, 448, 18}, {850, 440, 16}
}
for _, th in ipairs(thistles) do
  local x, y, h = th[1], th[2], th[3]
  b_rigger:load(p_straw_shade, 0.8)
  b_rigger:stroke({{x, y}, {x, y - h*0.6}, {x + rand(-2, 2), y - h}}, {pressure={0.65, 0.15}, ramps={0.05, 0.2}})
  b_rigger:load(p_straw_sharp, 0.85)
  b_rigger:stroke({{x - 3, y - h}, {x + 3, y - h}}, {pressure=0.4})
  b_rigger:stroke({{x, y - h - 2}, {x, y - h + 2}}, {pressure=0.4})
end

print("Ancient Veteran Oak, Companion Tree, and Crest Heathland Accents painted.")
